job: Fresh graduate in business, finance and accounting
name: Beth Weber

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for sitting down with me, Beth. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're independent: no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we're not selling anything. What you tell me is confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and what you really think. To start: tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I share a rented room with my friend Lotte in the city of Dunmere, and we split a tiny kitchen with two others. My mornings are job boards and emails to alumni, and in the afternoons I do three shifts a week at a café to cover my half of the rent. In the evenings I do a free online course on data analysis, because I'd rather be doing something than refreshing my inbox.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I did finance with an accounting strand, and I came out top of my year. I did a summer in audit at a mid-sized firm called Brandt Collins, then a winter placement in the finance team at a housing charity. The audit summer was long checklists and tick marks, and the charity taught me what the numbers are for, which is deciding who gets a flat. I loved that part more than I expected.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture, which we call AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that sounds about right, honestly. I use a tool to summarise long reports and it saves me twenty minutes, nothing dramatic. I'd tell friends to stop panicking and push firms to hire fairly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, my worry is the same as today. I have some debt, a couple of months of savings, and rent that eats most of my café pay. The world staying calm doesn't give me an offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep applying, aiming for audit and charity finance roles, and finish my data course by January. I'd ask Brandt Collins whether the manager who liked my work could pass my name on. I'd also ask my mum to be my safety net if I can't cover rent for a month, which I hate doing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, mainly. I know I'm good, and still every week without an offer makes me wonder if I'm missing something. A good chat with Lotte at the end of the day settles it a bit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you use AI tools now and then. What for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly for summaries and for tidying up cover letters. I don't paste any private data in, because a client's numbers shouldn't go to a company's server. I double-check anything it writes against the source, since it once invented a date in a report I was reading.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which bill bothers you most while you wait for an offer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rent first, honestly. My rent is due on the first and the café pays on the fifteenth, so there's always a gap. That's when I ask my mum for a loan, and she says don't worry and then worries. I'd love an offer just to end that circle.

say: I'd tell friends it's **modest**: handy for summaries, nothing dramatic.
I'd say firms should hire graduates **fairly** and stop leaving us guessing.
think: Off the record, my real worry is the **rent** and the empty inbox, not AI.
I do wonder, every unanswered week, whether I'm missing **something** obvious.
do: Finish the **data course** by January and keep applying to audit and charity finance roles.
Ask my old audit **manager** at Brandt Collins to pass my name on.
Lean on **Mum** for a rent gap only if I must.
feel: **Uneasy**, steadied by evenings with my flatmate Lotte.
S0.quote: My rent is due on the first and the café pays on the fifteenth, so there's always a gap.
fieldNote: Beth is practical: she uses tools in small, **checked** ways and keeps client data out.
Her unease is financial and immediate; the quiet scenario doesn't relieve it, so anxious fits.
Reluctance to ask her mother for money shows pride and care.

steps.text: Finish the online data analysis course by January
Ask my old audit manager to pass my name on
Borrow rent from Mum only for gaps

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we're watching entry-level work change in real time. Checking and sampling are exactly what a tool can do, so firms will hire fewer juniors. I'd push for rules that make companies say what they're automating.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the route I trained for gets smaller, but not shut. Audit firms will still want people, only fewer, and they'll want people who can explain findings. My worry is being one of the many top graduates fighting for fewer places.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd widen from audit to finance work in charities and councils, where the people side matters. I'd get properly good with two tools, one for spreadsheets and one for data, and put it on my CV with real examples. I'd also move my savings into a notice account so I don't dip into it for rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit anxious, but I'm still in the game. It feels like the rules are being changed while I'm sitting the exam, and I don't mind hard exams, I mind unfair ones.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What tasks in audit do you think software takes first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tick-and-check tasks first: matching invoices to bank lines, sampling transactions, drafting the first memo. At Brandt Collins that was about half my summer. What stayed human was the call with a client when a number looked wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you tell if a tool is really proven?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want to see it work on a real file in a team I trust, with someone responsible for the result. If my manager uses it and it saves time without causing errors for a few months, I'd believe it. If it's just a sales pitch, I'd wait.

say: I'd say entry-level work is **changing** and firms should be open about what they automate.
I'd back rules that make companies **explain** where tools replace people.
think: I think my route **shrinks** but doesn't close, and I'm competing with many top graduates.
I'm anxious about the rules changing mid-exam, which feels **unfair**.
do: Widen the search from audit to **charity and council** finance roles.
Get good at **two tools**, one for spreadsheets and one for data, with real CV examples.
Move savings into a **notice account** to protect them from rent dips.
feel: **Anxious** but still in the game, annoyed at unfair rules.
S1.quote: I don't mind hard exams, I mind unfair ones.
fieldNote: Beth names the tasks that go first from her own audit summer, which makes her view concrete.
She stays **evidence-minded**: she would trust a tool only after a team she trusts has used it.
Her instinct to widen toward people-centred finance links her charity placement to her plan.

steps.text: Apply to charity and council finance teams as well as audit
Build two worked examples with spreadsheet and data tools for my CV
Move savings into a notice account

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is exactly when we need public action. Two years is too short for any firm to retrain its people, so government has to step in with income support. I'd sign every petition and turn up to a meeting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think most of what I trained for goes within a couple of years. I'd feel like I'd spent four years learning a language and then found out nobody speaks it any more. I'd also be terrified for my mum, who's a nurse and would be fine, but I would be the one asking her for help.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop being picky and take anything with a payslip, café full-time if needed, to cover rent. I'd keep the data course going because it's cheap and might lead somewhere. And I'd get involved with a local group pushing for retraining money, because shouting alone is useless.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I can feel my chest tighten when I imagine the email saying not to apply any more. But I'd also feel strangely focused, like a deadline has finally been set.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Lotte that evening?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Lotte we should keep the room as long as possible and cook together, so we're cheaper. I'd say we both look at the same things, jobs, courses, groups, and share what we find. We'd cry a bit first, I'm sure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you do about rent if hiring stops?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Café full-time, probably forty hours, and cut everything else down to rent, food and phone. I'd tell the landlord early and ask for a month's grace if needed. If I can't cover it, I go home to my mum's for a while, which would feel like a step back.

say: I'd say **government** must step in with income support, because two years is too short for firms.
I'd sign petitions and join a group pushing for **retraining money**.
think: Privately I think most of what I trained for **disappears** within two years.
It'd feel like learning a language nobody speaks any more, and I'd be **frightened** about money.
do: Take **full-time café hours** to cover rent and stop being picky.
Keep the cheap **data course** going in case it leads somewhere.
Join a local group lobbying for **retraining funds**.
feel: **Alarmed**, with my chest tight, yet oddly focused.
S2.quote: I'd feel like I'd spent four years learning a language and then found out nobody speaks it any more.
fieldNote: The fast scenario breaks her measured style; she turns **defensive** and collective.
Her image of the lost language is vivid and honest about grief for her degree.
Practical about rent, but moving back to her mum's is a quiet, sore fallback.

steps.text: Work full-time at the café to cover the rent
Cut spending to rent, food and phone only
Join the local group asking for retraining funds
Ask my mum if I can move home if rent fails

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a window, and we should use it for policy, not panic. I'd tell friends to choose skills where people trust people, like advice, ethics and negotiation. I'd also say schools should start teaching how to work with tools now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel anxious but able to act. The warning lets me build a different footing, like moving into roles that explain and decide, rather than only check. I'd still worry that every other top graduate is doing the same.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take an entry job in a team that uses AI sensibly and ask to be on the projects where tools are brought in. I'd sit the professional accountancy exams, since a human signature will still be needed for a while. And I'd put away a fixed amount monthly so I'm never one month from trouble.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious but steady. It's like seeing a storm on the forecast. You can't stop it, but you can pack and know where the shelter is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you do with five years that you can't do with two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With five years I can build a record before the worst of it. I can do exams, a first job and a real network, instead of dashing for any job. With two I'd just be surviving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you decide whether to study further?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd study further only if a firm or a public scheme pays, because I don't want a second debt on top of the first. A master's is only worth it if it leads somewhere concrete. I'd ask three people working in the field before signing anything.

say: I'd say five years is a **window** for policy, not panic.
I'd tell friends to build skills where **people trust people**, like advice and ethics.
think: I'd feel anxious but **able to act**, because the warning lets me build new footing.
I worry every other top graduate will pick the same **safe** niche.
do: Take an entry job in a team that uses **tools sensibly** and volunteer for those projects.
Sit **professional exams**, since a human signature will still be needed for a while.
Save a **fixed amount** monthly so I'm never one month from trouble.
feel: **Anxious** but steady, like packing for a forecast storm.
S3.quote: A master's is only worth it if it leads somewhere concrete.
fieldNote: Time moves Beth from reacting to **building**; her plans are sequenced and checked.
She is wary of a second debt, so she limits further study to funded routes.
Sees the crowding risk: many top graduates will choose the same safe niche.

steps.text: Take an entry job on a team that uses AI sensibly
Save a fixed amount every month
Back national retraining policy by joining a local campaign

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is generous, so there's no excuse. Schools, firms and government can all plan, and I'd tell people to ask where the plan is. I'd also say it's a chance to make work better, not just cheaper.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be fairly settled. I'd have time to get qualified, work a few years, and maybe move toward advising people who need to understand the numbers. I'd still keep a second string, like data work, in case things move faster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish my data course, get a first job in audit or charity finance, and qualify. Around year three or four I'd start asking my firm to try tools properly. I'd also save for a deposit, slowly, and maybe stop sharing a room by 26.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine, mostly, with an edge of impatience. It's reassuring to have time, but time doesn't pay this month's rent. I'd keep reminding myself that the job search is the bit I control.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What might you try with ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Perhaps, but doing something different with the same skills, like advising small charities on budgets. I like the idea of finance as help, not only control. If the industry shrinks, I'd have the skills to move sideways.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you think you'd still be in finance by then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I might be, but not in the way I'm picturing now. A lot can change in ten years, including me. I'd keep learning what's proven and watch my own interests.

say: I'd say ten years is generous, so there's **no excuse** for not planning.
I'd say it's a chance to make work **better**, not just cheaper.
think: I'd feel fairly **settled**, with time to qualify and work a few years.
I'd keep a **second string**, like data work, in case things move faster.
do: Finish the data course and take a **first job** in audit or charity finance.
Ask my firm around year four to try **tools properly**.
Save for a **deposit** and stop sharing a room by 26.
feel: **Fine**, with an edge of impatience, because time doesn't pay this month's rent.
S4.quote: I like the idea of finance as help, not only control.
fieldNote: With a decade Beth turns hopeful and talks about **purpose**, tied to the charity placement.
Impatience persists because the present no-offer situation is unresolved.
She keeps a sideways route, which suits her steady profile.

steps.text: Finish the data course and take a first finance job
Ask my firm to try AI tools properly around year four
Save a deposit to stop sharing a room by 26

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 picture worries me most, because two years is too short to train for anything new while also paying rent. What would help is a bridge: paid retraining, some kind of basic income if firms cut fast, and honest advice from people already in the field. I'd also like firms to tell graduates plainly when they're not hiring juniors, so we stop guessing.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that I think my generation gets told two opposite things. One is that you must learn every tool, and the other is that none of it matters. I'd like someone to tell us what actually helps, with evidence.

headlineQuote: I can feel my chest tighten when I imagine the email saying not to apply any more.
portrait: **Beth** is a 23-year-old finance graduate, top of her class, with an audit internship and a charity placement.
She is progressive, wants **public support and regulation**, and judges new tools by evidence, using AI now and then.
She shares a rented room and works café shifts, so the **rent** is always on her mind.
In each scenario she moves in measured steps: learn what's proven, widen the search, and push for **fair rules**.
Her worry grows with speed: calm-ish with ten years, alarmed when the time to adjust disappears.
biggestWorry: The **2028 picture**, because two years is too short to retrain while also covering rent.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid retraining** and a basic income if firms cut fast.
Honest, evidence-based **advice** about what skills last, and firms saying plainly when they aren't hiring juniors.
